raw_case_text:
A five-year-old male non-Caucasian patient presented with fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis for 5 days. His past medical history was unremarkable, with normal psychomotor development, no family history neurological diseases and no consanguinity. The patient was born and lived in Ceara, northeast Brazil, and family reported no recent travels.
After 1 week he developed tonic-clonic seizures. Neurological examination was normal at this point. Complete blood count, liver functions and acute reactants were normal. Serologies for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, and toxoplasmosis were negative. Brain MRI was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 15 cells, protein 16.6 mg/dL and glucose 68 mg/dL. He was started on acyclovir and ceftriaxone.
Two weeks after seizure onset, he presented with dystonia (Video 1) and oromandibular dyskinesia. On physical examination the patient was awake, his speech output was decreased, pupils were normal. Cranial nerves examination was unremarkable. Muscle strength was symmetric and deep tendon reflexes were normoactive and symmetric. One week later he developed focal motor seizures followed by decreased level of consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea. EEG showed extreme delta brush and valproate and phenytoin were started. He also received methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulin with seizure resolution and improvement of level of consciousness, dysautonomia and orofacial dyskinesias within 2 weeks.
Anti-NMDAR antibodies were detected in serum (titer 1:25600) and CSF (titer 1:1024) after 3 weeks of symptom onset using tissue and cell-based assays as previously reported. CHIK serology was positive for both IgM and IgG, suggesting a recent infection. Dengue and Zika serologies were negative. CSF PCR for herpes viruses and arboviruses (CHIK, Dengue and Zika) were negative. Whole body CT and testis ultrasound were normal. Because of partial improvement (persistence of orofacial dyskinesias and impaired speech), the patient received rituximab and cyclophosphamide with good response. After 8 months he is seizure-free and has returned to school with only mild restlessness and inattention. Figure 1 describes the timeline of clinical features, investigation and treatment of the case report.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old non-Caucasian boy presented with a 5-day history of fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis, followed by new-onset tonic-clonic seizures 1 week later.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially experienced 5 days of fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis, followed 1 week later by tonic-clonic seizures. Two weeks after seizure onset, despite empiric acyclovir and ceftriaxone, he developed dystonia, oromandibular dyskinesia, and decreased speech output. One week later (3 weeks after seizure onset), he progressed to focal motor seizures, decreased consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history with normal psychomotor development. Born and resided in Ceara, northeast Brazil, with no recent travel, no consanguinity, and no family history of neurological disorders.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for initial fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis, followed by generalized and focal seizures, dystonia, oromandibular dyskinesia, reduced speech output, altered consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea.

objective.physical_examination: At initial seizure onset (week 1): neurological examination was normal. At 2 weeks post-seizure onset: awake with decreased speech output, dystonia, and oromandibular dyskinesia; pupils, cranial nerves, symmetric muscle strength, and normoactive symmetric deep tendon reflexes were normal. At 3 weeks post-seizure onset: focal motor seizures, decreased level of consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, liver function tests, and acute-phase reactants: normal. Viral and protozoal serologies (HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, and toxoplasmosis): negative. Testicular ultrasound: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: normal. Whole-body CT: normal. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: 15 cells/mm3, protein 16.6 mg/dL, glucose 68 mg/dL; CSF PCR negative for herpesviruses and arboviruses (chikungunya, dengue, and Zika). Electroencephalography (EEG): extreme delta brush pattern. Autoimmune encephalitis panel (3 weeks post-onset): anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (anti-NMDAR) antibodies strongly positive in serum (titer 1:25,600) and CSF (titer 1:1,024) by tissue and cell-based assays.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Post-infectious anti-NMDAR autoimmune encephalitis triggered by recent chikungunya virus infection. Direct viral CNS infection (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV, dengue, Zika, and CSF CHIKV RNA) and paraneoplastic teratoma/tumors were excluded. Confirmation: Positive serum chikungunya IgM and IgG serology, characteristic EEG extreme delta brush pattern, and high-titer anti-NMDAR antibodies in serum (1:25,600) and CSF (1:1,024). Management and outcome: Initially treated with empiric acyclovir, ceftriaxone, valproate, and phenytoin. Following diagnosis of anti-NMDAR encephalitis, first-line immunotherapy with IV methylprednisolone and IVIG resolved the seizures, dysautonomia, and consciousness impairment within 2 weeks; due to persistent orofacial dyskinesias and speech impairment, second-line rituximab and cyclophosphamide were administered with a strong clinical response. At 8-month follow-up, the child was seizure-free and back in school with only mild residual restlessness and inattention.
